p: Um, I don't know the exact time. I will get back to you on that.

Alright. I'm now gonna move on to MTA's reduced fare— Reduced Fare program. Fair Fares is not the only program that offers half-price transit fares to qualifying city residents. The other program is the MTA's Reduced Fare program, which is a separate program that offers a 50% discount to New Yorkers that are 65 years or older or that have a qualifying disability. How often do MTA and HRA hear from New Yorkers who are confused about the differences between the city's Fair Fares program and the MTA's separate reduced fare program?

Um, as far as, I mean, confusion, um, I mean, with Reduced Fare, we have about 1.5 million, um, customers enrolled in that

program and they can visit our various— the 30 customer service centers, as well as Stone Street and our mobile units, um, to, to get information and sign up. Um, and that is a distinct program, you know, that has been marketed to those who are 65 or older, or, um, with a disability. Um, as far as Fair Fares, as we know and the purposes that why we're here today is about, you know, this is a program that needs more robust, um, engagement and, and, and program awareness, um, given that there are far more people eligible for the program but far less people enrolled.
What happens if someone comes to a Fair Fares office to enroll in the program, but HRA determines that the person only qualifies for the MTA's reduced fare program?

So I could only speak about our programmatic engagement that happens within the system. Um, you know, on average when we do these events, I mean, we have— like, if it's an in-station transit talk, we sign up on average about 25 or up to 50 participants. Um, and when— if someone is not, um, eligible, whether it is, you know, for— because

their income is not, um, it's, it's over the threshold, or they don't have the information, we have a team, uh, member who follows up with them.
Likewise for the MTA, what happens if someone comes to an MTA customer service center to apply for the reduced fare program but is only eligible to participate in Fair Fares?

So, as I mentioned, we arm our, um, customer service reps with lots of handouts, um, and, and information, and we have the, uh, kiosks that are literally, um, next to the, the, um, customer service centers, and we encourage them to sign up, um, and start the application.

Public transit is essential for New York— New Yorkers' access to jobs, schools, healthcare, childcare, and other services. Lower-income New Yorkers are more dependent on public transportation than higher-income households, and transportation costs have continued to rise over time. How does the MTA evaluate the role of Fair Fares in addressing transportation affordability?

Well, it's part of a bigger equation, which is, you know, the overall

affordability of the transit system. Um, and as I said in the— at the start, it's, it's very much what makes New York affordable. You can come to the city, you're not buying a car, and you have access to the entire city. Um, what we've done over the last few years on student OMNY, expanding it from a couple times a day during the school year to 4 times a day, 7 days a week throughout the year. City Ticket, which was a weekend-only, uh, product for 20-something years, now it's available all week long. It's completely changed what's available to people. So yeah, this is front and center, the affordability of transit. But, but we, you know, we, we're always looking for finding more affordable products, getting this product you know, making it available to New Yorkers. And so Fair Fares is a part of that but what we see and what we found in our study is if you have 60% of the people who have signed up, only 60% are active. These are the people who have gone out of their way to sign up. And they're the ones that— so talking about the people who haven't signed up, I think we get an idea. It means that the people who are signed up are not using the system as much as

they need to, or they just don't— they're not making those trips. If you change the eligibility threshold and bring in those folks who are going to minimum wage plus jobs, I think you're going to really hit affordability and get more people into this program, and word will spread.

Um, if I could just add to John's response, I think what's— what we are really focused on is, um, widening the net for this tool to reach even more New Yorkers. So I think one of the decisions the Council is considering is whether you go deeper on affordability for— in a world of limited resources and funding, deeper for a smaller number of people, or increase affordability to a wider number of people as you, you know, have those budget negotiations with the Administration. I think we are very supportive of trying to make this tool as accessible to as many people as possible.
Thank you. Does the MTA collect data on how Fair Fares affects participants' access to work, school, medical care, food benefits, or other essential services?

Yes, so I think, um, you know, and we're happy to continue exploring this in more

detailed ways, but some of the preliminary research that we shared with you is looking at where people are tapping, um, first thing in the morning, and where they're tapping at the p.m. peak., and we can really try to break that down and understand those locations in a really granular way. But it really helps us understand what the purpose of travel— or we can make some, you know, assumptions about the purpose of travel based on these locations, um, without directly speaking to the people who are enrolled through HRA's program.
Yeah, it would be interesting to see that data for sure at a granular level.
Yeah, happy to. Yeah, happy to share.
And then we can work with that.
Yeah, absolutely.
Work with you guys on that, that would be great. Does MTA target its outreach to neighborhoods with high poverty rates and high transit dependence? If so, how?

Yeah, um, absolutely. I mean, we, you know, working with the, the policy team, um,

with lots of data gathering, we— and also, um, with engagement from— with our government relations team and working with electeds and community stakeholders, identifying those, um, location where there are large pockets of eligibility, um, and we go out into the system prior to our arrival doing, um, lots of effort to get the word out by way of the electeds, the community boards, um, or trusted CBOs and community partners to let them know that we are in, um, the neighborhood or in the community to sign up and enroll folks.
Thank you for that. I'm now gonna turn it over to my Co-Chair, Council Member Kristal Hudson.

Thank you so much, Chair. Um, upon approval, Fair Fares participants may receive a Fair Fares OMNY card through the mail or apply the discount directly to an existing OMNY card, bank card, or mobile wallet. When money is added to a Fair Fares OMNY Card, half of the current fare is deducted each time the card is tapped. If a Fair Fares enrollee takes 12 paid trips within a 7-day period with the same card, they automatically receive free rides for the rest of the week. How many Fair

Fares participants currently use Fair Fares OMNY Cards?

Uh, thank you for the question. I think we addressed this, um, while you weren’t in the room, but we have— we are now at close to a, like, 98.5% transition to Tap-and-Ride and that covers all of our physical fare media programs. Essentially, what's left are, like, around 2% for people who are paying with coins on the bus and a very small number of our own employees who still have Metro Cards. So, the— all of these programs have already transitioned to physical OMNY fare media.
And to Chairman Abreu's, your previous, um, question, we have 5,000— um, Access-A-Ride customers that are currently enrolled in Fair Fares.

Thank you. Forgive me just one second. Thank you. We're just comparing notes here. Um, okay. The Council needs reliable data to evaluate whether Fair Fares is reaching eligible New Yorkers, reducing transportation hardship, and operating efficiently. Do you have an understanding of MTA ridership at different income levels?

So, um, I would just, like, generally characterize the ways we understand our riders are by speaking with them in our surveys, or where they can tell us that information about themselves and demographic characteristics. And then the other way we track folks, um, or try to understand their travel patterns is through the way they pay and where they're paying and what time of day. Um, with transactions, we don't know anything about people's demographics or their income levels other than those who are already in income-restricted programs like Fair Fares. Um, but we do have information about, uh, you know, the demographics and travel proclivities of our riders through survey data.

Okay, that's helpful. Thank you. Um, what do you expect, or what does the MTA expect you would expect the difference in ridership to be between someone making 150 to 200% of the federal poverty level and someone below 150%? Do you have any idea?

Yeah, I don't know that we have an exact projection. I just think that we would

expect you would reach more people who would ride more frequently. Uh, in the brief that we shared with you all, you can see that, um, the travel patterns of Fair Fares enrollees today already mimics the a.m., p.m. peak of the broader system with slightly more off-peak travel. I think you're just reaching more working New Yorkers because the income threshold today is so low.

And Chair, I would just add that the- just the reality of the way our system works, when you see weekday ridership versus Saturday and Sunday, you- I mean, you have a significant drop-off, students and people who are coming to and going from work. Um, and so the higher the threshold, I think you're capturing people who are going to jobs, um, more so than you do today, where it would either be someone who's working part-time, um, or, or maybe they're not working, or they're doing something, you know, in the neighborhood, local. So, um, yeah, I think you would see, uh, the sort of growth that you would see whenever you pull in people who are coming to and going from work.
Thank you for that. Do you know on average what percent of New Yorkers living below the federal poverty line use public transit?

Yeah, I mean, I think the census statistics are mostly about how you commute to and from work. We have some of that in our survey data for— that includes leisure and other forms of travel, so we can get back to you on the specific, like, share relative to the poverty line.

That would be helpful. Thank you. The MTA's data on Fair Fares rides by station shows that subway ridership is almost twice that of bus ridership. Do you know why this might be the case, and is this consistent with public transit ridership for non-Fair Fares users?

Yes, that is generally consistent. It is a much higher share— I would say slightly higher share of Fair Fares users than the rest of the system use the bus and make bus-to-subway transfers, but it's not a big differential, which is in, I think, one of the, um, charts or graphs that we shared with you all.

Okay, thank you. How does the MTA expect the weekly ridership of those on the

Fair Fares program to change if Fair Fares changes to a 100% discount for those who qualify?

I don't think we know that. I think, you know, just going back to how I responded to a couple of questions ago, we don't know how much usage is, um, you know, what, what usage possibilities there are with somebody who's earning below 100%, um, federal poverty. Uh, we already know that at the rate it is today, 150%, there's 40% who aren't active who have enrolled. So it suggests that that is a factor, and that going for getting people who are going to and from work will- will make that number pop more than, um, as Dara sort of went through the trade-off that elected officials and policymakers face, um so.

Thank you. Um, and then just a couple questions about legislation. So for Resolution Number 143, unlimited transfers within 2 hours, does the MTA have an estimate of how many riders would benefit from this policy?

Um, no, but I would say there is like, a couple of different elements to that. So one, on the subway system, it would be very— you know, you can already make unlimited transfers as

long as you're within the system. So if the question is, do you do unlimited travel within 2 hours, we— and- and it's part of transfers, we would need a way for folks to be able to tap out in order to register that as a transfer if you were going to make some kind of out-of-system transfer, and we don't have that validator technology installed today, so that would be a pretty significant change to the way the subway system operates. On the bus, we are piloting this on the Queens Bus Network redesign, which is a time-limited, uh, window of a universal transfer, and for that, I think the bus is a little bit— because of the technology and directionality that we're able to understand when people tap onto those modes, it's a little bit more feasible, but we're still trying to understand how people are using that and what the broader implication would be for the full system.
Okay and then, could unlimited transfers be implemented through OMNY without major changes, you think?
It would require a lot of programming, I think, to understand this.

Yeah but in addition to complicated programming, there's complicated budgeting, um, attached to that, um, just because with unlimited— it's not necessarily an unlimited transfer, it's unlimited trips. That's a different thing altogether, um, where you have, you have real budgetary consequences that would have to be addressed if that policy decision were to be advanced. That's why we've always done it with the transfer, the transfer that you can get within system, obviously, that we're all familiar with, and then the bus to subway transfer. That didn't always exist. It's another, you know, it's an amazing thing looking back in time that there was a time when people paid, you know, 2 fares.
Yep.
Remember? So, um, so, but I just would caution that there is, there are a number of different issues related to that- that we have to deal with.

Yeah and I guess, um, one example that I can think of that's specific to my district is, and one of my biggest gripes with the

Barclays Center, um, that when it, when that whole development came about, Atlantic Yards, not specifically the Barclays Center, I shouldn't say that, but with Atlantic Yards, was they invested all of this money into redesigning the subway station directly underneath the Barclays Center, but we have, within just a few blocks, a G train station, a C train station, and there was no tunnel created to connect people within those— within that system. And that, that, um, walk, I would estimate, to be similar or shorter than the walk you have to do at Time Square or something, you know, to move through. And so I guess that's— it's thinking about— I would think about trips as transfers, not necessarily saying you're taking the train to go to work, then you're hanging— you know, you're spending the day at work, and then you're unlimited, you know, ride to go somewhere else, or for lunch, or whatever. But really more so if there's not a direct connection available between different train routes, you know, thinking about transfers available.
Yeah.
And so maybe there's like a way to geo-target or something that within a certain area you can—
Yeah. So as opposed to a universal on-time transfer period.
Yeah and this is just my own personal question. I don't want to— this is not my bill, it's not my legislation. I don't want to speak on behalf of the sponsor, but I'm just, you know—

Yeah. Well, so the good news is with, uh, Tap and Ride, it's, you know, there's so much more possible, and it's— and that is, uh, Chair, something that we are, we are aware of, and we have people who are looking at exactly that sort of thing. So we should talk more about it.
I look forward to it and I'll, uh, turn it back over to Chair Abreu, and also want to acknowledge that we've been joined by Council Member Nurse. Thank you.

These are my last set of questions. What happens when someone who is part of the Fair Fares program hits 65 and transitions out of the Fair Fares program? How does HRA or MTA coordinate, if at all, to ensure a seamless and

timeless transition from the Fair Fares program to the Reduced Fare program?

Seamless? Um, so I would not say it's seamless. I mean, again, um, you know, it, it— there can and should be, um, better coordination as, as, uh, Fair Fare participants are aging out of the program and introducing and promoting and encouraging, um, folks to, um, transition over to Fair Fares. And that is something that we can all collectively do a better job in coordinating.

Yeah, and it's about getting information— I mean, it's, it's a date and time. So people know when they're turning. So getting that information into the hands of people who are in Fair Fares who are coming up on that age. We do that with seniors. We are, we are, you know, asking them always to start preparing and planning. And so many of them are, are so, you know, I have my own parents, they're so aware of it. It's like, I'm gonna have that in day one. So, um, that, that window of somebody turning 64 and then 65 going on to, uh, Reduced Fare. It's, it's— we, we gotta, we gotta all be better there. That's, that should—

I really appreciate you guys just being straight up honest about that because I remember when I was, uh, at the rally this morning, one of the advocates— I think she's here in the audience, uh, with the red hair back there um-
Deborah Greif.
What’s your name?
Deborah Greif.

Uh, Deborah, thank you. You know, she mentioned to me that it doesn't make sense that when you're 64 years old as part of Fair Fares and you turn 65, you have to enter an entirely new, different program And I know it was a state-run program. But for these folks who benefit from this, they should just be able to have a seamless transition. I would even argue it should just be automatic. If you're part of Fair Fares and you turn 65, you should be automatically enrolled into Reduced Fare program. But if we can't do that, we need to find a way to coordinate better from HRA to the MTA. And so I'm glad that there's a sense of urgency here already. And I think it would make— it would improve the quality of life and also increase access to our mass transit system for those who really need it.

So thank you so much for testifying.

So there's, there's, you know, there is complications with that and there's litigation involved. So it's— but I, you know, we will get back to you on more on, on that transition and making sure it's smooth.
Let's keep talking. Thank you Chair.

Excellent. Thank you so much. We are going to move to public testimony, but I do want to thank you and just note for the record that you are not, um, legally mandated to be here. And so we do really appreciate your time, um, and willingness to answer the questions and to partner with us. So thank you.
Thanks for having us.

Thank you. Okay, we are now opening the hearing for public testimony, and I wanna remind members of the public that this is a government proceeding and that decorum shall be observed at all times. As such, members of the public shall remain silent at all times. The witness table is reserved for people who wish to testify. No

video recording or photography is allowed from the witness table. Further, members of the public may not present audio or video recordings as testimony, but may submit transcripts of such recordings to the Sergeant-at-Arms for inclusion in the hearing record. If you wish to speak at today's hearing, please fill out an appearance card with the Sergeant-at-Arms and wait to be recognized. When recognized, you will have 2 minutes to speak on the oversight topic, Fair Fares or on Introduction 248, Introduction 825, Resolution 52, or Resolution 143. If you have a written statement or additional written testimony you wish to submit for the record, please provide a copy of that testimony to the Sergeant-at-Arms. You may also email written testimony to testimony@council.nyc.gov within 72 hours of this hearing. Audio and video recordings will not be accepted. And I want to ask if Little Flores is here. No. Okay. So the first panel— the first panel will be Eduardo Rodriguez, Ruldolph Pongnon, apologies. Marie Pierre, Tenaiya Ortiz-Long. Thank you, thank

you, and we'll just start at my left, your right, at the end of the table here. You can begin when you're ready. You can begin when you're ready. You want to just hit the microphone? Just hit the button at the bottom. Perfect, thank you.

Uh, good afternoon Council. Uh, thank you for, uh, holding this hearing and the opportunity to be heard. My name is Eduardo Rodriguez on behalf of Freedom Agenda and the campaign to close Rikers Island. I'm here to support Riders Alliance because I acknowledge the connection between being economically disadvantaged and, um, attempting to make a reintegration successfully. The burden of hardship associated with accessing public transportation has not allowed me to maintain, uh, certain obligations as a result of my release. Um, I'm gonna read a script that I worked on all week, uh, because I only— I'm limited with time. Um, as a justice-impacted individual, I recall my inability to afford public transportation, leaving me feeling entrapped, prejudiced, targeted, and conditioned for criminalization. I recently collaborated with Riders Alliance in the push to improve access to public transportation

for all New Yorkers through a host of efforts because it never made sense to me that a warrant would be issued for my arrest because I couldn't afford to travel to a legal appointment, whether it be court, probation, parole, community service, jury duty, or being presented with the dilemma of having to choose between the most important meal of the day— for me, it's coffee and a bagel— or hopping the turnstile at the risk of being ticketed because I was being targeted for arrest or paying my fare. I remember having to hop a turnstile to get to an interview for employment that only required that I turn in documents. I never made it to the interview. Instead, I wound up in cuffs. My eager plea to be released so I could make it to the interview led the officer to believe that I was evading the law. He held me in hopes that a warrant would pop up in the system. Some things never change. About 2 weeks ago, as I was leaving a Riders Alliance meeting that prepared me for this hearing, I entered the Fulton Street Train Station, tapped my OMNY card courtesy of Riders Alliance, it wasn't until I turned the corner onto

the platform that I noticed an officer peering around the corner waiting for someone to beat the fare. Most New Yorkers struggle with the burden of hardship associated with the cost of public transportation. Denying New Yorkers access to public transportation limits our citizens' rights to liberty, interests, and pursuit of happiness. No one should face arrest, miss opportunities, or be pushed deeper into hardship simply because they cannot afford to swipe into a subway system that this city depends on. I urge City Council to act now and make Fairs Fare truly fair for the millions of New Yorkers who keep this city moving every day. Thank you.
Thank you so much for your testimony.

Good morning, Chair and members of the Committee. My name is Tenaiya Ortiz-Long. I'm a lifelong New Yorker. I've lived in Brooklyn, Queens, and now the Bronx. I'm here today to advocate for affordable transit and the expansion of Fair Fares. In my lifetime, I've watched the fare go from $2.25 to $3. That 75— 75-cent increase may sound

small, but it adds up, and it's pricing people out. Right now, I qualify for Fair Fares, but the moment I get a full-time minimum wage job at $17 an hour, I will lose that support. After taxes, that is about $28,000 a year, just over the current eligibility cutoff for around $23,000 a year. Somehow that's considered too much to qualify, even though it's nowhere near enough to survive in this city. Let's be real about math. Rent for a studio can be $1,800 a month. Phone bill is around $120. Wi-Fi, $75. Groceries can range from $200 to $600. Utilities added can be another $150 to $300, and the costs keep rising. After paying for basic needs, there's nothing left. In fact, I'd be in the negative before even paying for transit. At 21, I hopped the turnstile after work because I had no money left and was waiting to get paid. Instead of getting home safely, I was given a $100 ticket and threatened with arrest. I was forced to choose between being stranded or being criminalized. That is not a real choice. Fair Fare should not disappear the moment someone starts earning slightly more.

I'm asking you to expand it so working people are not punished for trying to get ahead. Thank you for listening to a New Yorker who just wants to afford to stay in the city she calls home.
Thank you so much for your testimony.

Uh, I want to, uh, thank the, uh, honorable members of the City Council for, uh, giving me the opportunity to, um, provide my testimony. Um, I was particularly inspired, uh, to come here to speak on behalf of, uh, the swath of, uh, New Yorkers who, um, are experiencing abject poverty. Um, my name's, uh, Ruldolph Pongnon, and, um, it wasn't easy for me to, uh, show up here. I'm, I'm feeling a bit, uh, emasculated, ashamed, and, uh, depressed by, uh, my current, uh, circumstance. And, um, I've been in, uh, I've been an activist since, uh, 2016, and, uh, I've dedicated myself to, uh, speaking truth to power. Uh, so while I had consternations about showing up here, um, and, uh, talking about, uh, the, uh, the ugly reality of living in, uh, abject poverty in New York city. Um, someone has to do it, and um, one of

the commandments that I live by is, uh, be the change that you seek and so I'm here. Uh, I haven't worked, uh, since the shutdown of April of, uh, 2020. Uh, I did— I used to have a career. Uh, I have a bachelor's degree in Business Administration with, uh, a major in Accounting. Um, I, uh, I was eventually, um, I was diagnosed in, uh, I was diagnosed with Chronic Fatigue Syndrome, uh, in my mid-30s, and I have other, uh, comorbidities. Uh, I've also been, uh, diagnosed with, um, major depressive disorder, uh, generalized anxiety disorder, um, adult selective mutism, sleep apnea, and, uh, ADHD. And, um, eventually all of this, uh, pushed me out of the workforce. Um, I have, however, been making, uh, incremental improvements over the years. And, um, I have, uh, a little more, uh, confidence— confidence that I, um, will be able to eventually have a, ah, relatively normal standard of living. Um, what I wanna say is that, um, anyone, uh, like myself, who's on cash assistance, um, I believe they should receive, um, a free, uh, Fair Fare, uh, OMNY card. Um, and, uh, I think it would be bad policy not to do it. Um, I think it would be

inhumane, and I think, um, it, it would punish the poor simply for being poor. What I get from, uh, cash assistance, which is my, um, sole source of income, uh, I get $59.05 twice a week. So that comes up to $118.10— I'm sorry, uh, twice a month. I'm sorry. I get $59.05 twice a month, and that comes up to, um, $118.10. That's my only, uh, source of income. Um, so my, uh, my phone bill and internet, uh, that comes up— while it's - it's discounted, it comes up to roughly, uh, $15, um, a month. Uh, doing the laundry, on a weekly basis for a month about $50, and, um, uh, incidentals, toiletries, cleaning supplies, uh, pest control, roaches and rats, uh, another $50. So I'm already at $150 and, um, my monthly income is $118.10. Um, so this is, uh, this is how this whole dynamic, uh, works out for me in practice. Um, I don't actually do the laundry, uh, every week, uh, even if I could. Um, my incidentals, I address that only when it's, uh, absolutely necessary, so when I'm in a situation where, uh, I'm running out of a bar of soap, then I gotta go buy another bar of soap. And, uh, just gotta be that frugal.

Um, as far as my Fair Fares, uh, Reduced fare Fair Fare card, um, so I— whenever I put money on it, I put, uh, $10 on the card, and, um, I, I call it my, uh, what-if money. And the reason why I call it my what-if money, it's, um—
Excuse me, you're gonna have to— if you could just wrap up shortly. Thank you.

Yes, uh, yes, uh, so the reason I, I call it my what-if money is in case, um, I, I'm in the subway and I see law enforcement, and I don't have time to beg for a swipe, so then I use my, uh, my Fair Fare, uh, card. And, um, I, I can't imagine if I had to use, uh, public transportation every day. And, um, I, I hope the- my testimony encourages you to make this program, uh, more robust and thank you for the time.
Thank you so much for your testimony.

Hi, good afternoon. Um, my name is Marie Nadine Pierre. I just want to preface what I'm about to read just briefly, inspired by my co-panelists. Um, I was born in New— in Brooklyn to immigrants from Haiti. Hard work is part of our DNA, and I've actually worked since I was 14. I never

thought I'd be in a low-wealth situation because I did earn a college degree at 20, and I went to earn my master's degree at UC Berkeley and went on to an Ivy League institution for a doctorate. I've attempted 3 doctorates so far, but I'm still in the low-wealth cat— category, most likely because of my lifestyle in this city. That keeps changing and welcoming new people that look more like the, the, um, the neoliberal economy prefers to hire in either service sector or the private sector. So it's been impossible to get a job. I lost my 4 children. We was— we stayed in a family shelter in, um, in Queens, and they wouldn't keep us after 3 months. So my poverty issues have been enormous, even though I did everything I was supposed to since I was 16 years old. So, um, right now I end up having to beg online and on the streets for— for— to people to— for money to afford the basics. I am on HRA benefits, but they are not enough, because I suffer from a bunch of different problems, health problems, because my immune system has deteriorated over the years, and I require a lot of vitamins that the insurance does not

cover, so I have to buy those out of pocket. This is what I wrote. Um, my name is Marie Nadine Pierre, and I live in New York City. I support expanding Fair Fares because affordable transit directly affects my ability to meet basic needs. I rely on the subway and bus to get to medical appointments in Manhattan and Queens, as well as Brooklyn. And when I cannot afford the fare, I have to- I have had to ask other riders for a swipe, including this morning to get here. No one should have to depend on strangers to just to reach- to reach necessary healthcare. Fair Fares also helps people stay connected to work and opportunity. The cost of transportation can keep me from job searching, attending interviews, and participating fully in my community. I currently have a reduced fare, but I feel that a free fare would let me travel consistently and with dignity while I work to stabilize my income. I respectfully urge the Committee to expand Fair Fares by increasing the income limit to at least 300% of the federal poverty level, so more low-income and near-poor New Yorkers like me can afford to ride.

Fair Fare assistance is an investment in public health, access to employment, and equity. Thank you for your consideration.

Thank you so much. And I want to thank you all, uh, again for your testimony. I know it's not always easy to come up in front of a panel, um, and put on the public record your circumstances and situations, but one of the many reasons why we always ask for directly impacted folks to go first is because we think it's incredibly important for people to hear your testimony. Um, and so thank you again. We should not be criminalizing poverty. Um, and so I know that, you know, the City Council will do everything we can to work directly with the Administration to address some of the issues that you all have brought up here today. So thank you again for your time.
I agree with our Co-Chair and everything she said.
Okay, our next two panelists are from the Independent Budget Office, Claire Salant and Emily Promick— Pramik, apologies, um, and our general counsel will swear you both in.

Now, in accordance with the rules of the Council, I will administer the affirmation to the witnesses from the Independent Budget Office. Please raise your right hand. Do you affirm to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth in your testimony before this Committee and to respond honestly to Council Member questions.
